There's been a huge amount of work done studying systems that work as punishment vs rehabilitation. I don't think there's really any 'best' study/studies. The evidence is unusually clear for a social sciences question: rehabilitation systems are vastly more effective than purely punitive systems. As somebody else mentioned here non-Norwegians often mock Norway's penal system since things from societies used to punishment can look strange. Eg - mass murderer Anders Breivik received 20 years (which can be extended as necessary if he is still deemed a danger) and has been able to successfully petition to receive things like a video game console in his cell. However, Norway's prison system results in some of the lowest recidivism rates in the world. They do not focus on punishing the criminals but trying to reform them to be proper members of society upon their release.

I think this is intuitive as well once you consider things beyond a surface level. Humans are incredibly adaptable. When you put somebody through horrific conditions for a decade or more they're not going to be the same person when they come out. They're going to have grown hard, grown to hate the people and the system that put them here, and adapted to live in a system where sociopathic behavior is a means to survival. And now you put them back out into civilized society. Is this new person with these new adaptions going to be more or less fit for society? More or less likely to resort to crime?
